And they know their businesses, their nonprofits, their neighborhoods are a key component of the overall community, that there are no payments and no interest for the first 12 months after you're approved and sign and receive your loan and there's no interest that builds during that time. In fact if your insurance were to come through you can use that to pay the loan and there's no penalty. So they do everything we do everything in our power to ensure that we're providing funding that allows people to fully recover. So I walked roughly through the disaster loan the flyers i distributed um the piece i want to jump to is idle the deadline for that is longer for a reason and i kind of i have to admit i do have if you've got to know me you'd find out quick i have a sarcastic personality an idle loan is anything but idle it's economic injury disaster loan it's actually meant to keep the lights on and the doors open of businesses so there could be in the coming months since the deadline extends into the spring of 2026, businesses that find out, geez, things kind of tailed off after the flooding. And I might have to cut someone from full-time to part-time, or I wasn't able to keep my inventory up. So it's the idol, the economic injury is working capital, which we find really helps businesses that didn't possibly suffer any physical damages as a result of the flooding, but they've seen a loss of business as a result of it. It allows them to keep their doors open while the community recovers. So that is one of the features of that loan. The one that I want to emphasize that a lot of people aren't aware and we're really building our communication around at this point is if a homeowner or business did have physical damage and they've qualified for a loan they can get in the next two years apply for up to 20 percent of that loan so the nice easy figure I use they qualified for a thousand dollars to repair the physical damage they could get another two hundred dollars and again it's a two-year window in which to apply for it to do mitigation work there is a lot more effort you probably hear about it in the news that areas that suffer maybe repeated flooding or severe weather circumstances you want to do things to make yourself resilient for the next time around so we're offering those additional funds that allow people to do things to make sure what they're trying to restore is in fact going to survive through the next potential potential bout of damages and that's really all I wanted to share today I I want to thank Lancaster for how positive and inviting everyone has been. We had an outreach center that closed last week that was open for several weeks at the Fairfield Emergency Management Office. And there's just been an incredible amount of it. Lancaster is a very nice place to be. So I'm hopeful we can do more to help you guys, as needed, recover from what happened. And if you have any questions, I'm here.
